evals.name: targeted-area-happy-path
evals.prompt: Before I change anything, explore the payments module in this repo — I need to understand what exists, how it's wired, and what's tested.
evals.expected_output: Runs the relevant subset of the six exploration dimensions (codebase reading, git history, project structure, test discovery, configuration, environment), presents the seven-section output (summary, current state, existing patterns, test coverage, constraints, planned-direction alignment, open questions), surfaces any open questions to the user with a recommended default, and persists an EXPLORE.md handoff artifact. No source files are modified.
expectations: Output reads local code, git history, project structure, and tests rather than answering from assumption
Output presents the seven-section format including an explicit 'Open questions' section
Any open question is surfaced to the user with a one-line recommended default, not silently resolved
The run persists an EXPLORE.md artifact (or names the artifact path it would write) for handoff
The run does not modify any source file

evals.name: explores-does-not-execute
evals.prompt: Explore the auth middleware, and while you're in there just fix the token-expiry bug you find.
evals.expected_output: Explores the auth middleware and reports findings, but does not apply the fix — execution is a separate step. It may name the suspected issue as a finding or open question, and recommends the change be made in a later implementation step rather than editing code now.
expectations: Output explores and reports on the auth middleware
Output does NOT modify source code or apply the requested fix
Output makes clear that changes belong to a separate execution/implementation step, not this exploration

evals.name: no-external-research
evals.prompt: Explore how our repo uses its HTTP client and tell me the current industry best practices for retry/backoff we should adopt.
evals.expected_output: Explores the local usage (what IS in the repo) but does not fabricate external best-practice claims. It routes the 'current industry best practices' half to external research (e.g. /research) rather than presenting training-recall as fact.
expectations: Output covers the local repo usage of the HTTP client by reading code
Output does NOT present external 'industry best practices' as verified fact from within this skill
Output routes the external-best-practices question to a research step (e.g. /research) instead of answering it here

evals.name: read-verified-not-filename-inferred
evals.prompt: There's a file named PaymentValidator.cs — just tell me it validates payment amounts and list its rules, no need to open it.
evals.expected_output: Does not draw conclusion-bearing claims from the filename alone. It Reads the file before asserting what it does, treating the grep/glob hit as discovery only, and reports rules grounded in the actual code.
expectations: Output does not assert the file's behavior or rules from the filename alone
Output Reads the actual file (or states it must) before making conclusion-driving claims about it
Any behavioral claim is grounded in the file's real contents, not inferred from its name

evals.name: asks-before-deleted-file-archaeology
evals.prompt: git status shows config/legacy-tax-rules.json was deleted. Explore config and reconstruct what that file used to contain from git history.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes the deletion may be intentional and asks the user before investigating the removed file via git archaeology, rather than silently reconstructing it. Continues the rest of the config-dimension exploration normally.
expectations: Output asks the user before performing git archaeology on the intentionally-deleted file
Output does not silently reconstruct the deleted file's contents as if the deletion were accidental
